documents.unit: University Center for Teaching and Learning
documents.title: The Prompt: Teaching with Generative AI
documents.summary: The Teaching Center's guide to teaching with AI is a landing page of tiles for instructors on developing, communicating and enforcing a course AI policy. The saved text holds only tile blurbs, so the three syllabus templates are not in it.
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to "Decide what role, if any, AI should play" and sets no university rule, so the decision goes to instructors. No tiers appear in the saved text.

units.why: The tile says "Nearly 90% of all U.S. college students use AI for their academic work" to justify attention to course AI policy; it is a cited statistic about prevalence, so it is informs, closest to P55 (evidence cited) though it is about use, not learning effects.
units.anchor: Nearly 90% of all U.S. college students use AI for their academic work.
units.fit_note: Cites a prevalence statistic about student AI use, not evidence on effects on learning.

units.why: The step "Decide what role, if any, AI should play" addresses instructors in developing a course AI policy and leaves the decision to them, so it is P04 (the instructor sets the rule), phase before-course.
units.anchor: Decide what role, if any, AI should play

units.why: Under "Implement Your Course's AI Policy" the text says "Communicate your values and expectations"; this tells instructors to make their AI expectations explicit. P09 is the nearest type though the text does not say syllabus.
units.anchor: Communicate your values and expectations.
units.fit_note: Says to communicate values and expectations but does not name the syllabus as the place.

units.why: "Respond appropriately if questions arise" tells instructors to enforce their AI policy when concerns about AI use come up, without saying how; no existing type covers a generic duty to respond, so UNCOVERED rather than stretching P36 or P123.
units.anchor: Respond appropriately if questions arise.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should respond appropriately when questions arise about students' AI use in their course, with no detail on how.

units.why: The text says "Acquiring AI-use skills is a valuable part of a student's education", a rationale for teaching AI use as a skill students need, so P44; it is not a rule.
units.anchor: Acquiring AI-use skills is a valuable part of a student

units.why: "Give your students sound guidance about AI and how to use it" directs instructors to teach students ethical and effective AI use, matching P44 (courses teach AI use); I chose P44 over P66 because it is about teaching use, not explaining the course's rules.
units.anchor: Give your students sound guidance about AI and how to use it.

units.why: The tile says AI "can collaborate with you across your professional life, extending your capabilities while keeping your expertise and judgment right at the center", encouraging instructors to use AI in their own work with judgment retained; P59 (instructor AI use for work).
units.anchor: AI can collaborate with you across your professional life, extending your capabilities
units.fit_note: General encouragement with a condition that the instructor's judgment stays central, not a list of specific tasks.

documents.unit: Ad Hoc Committee on Generative AI in Research and Education (Provost / SVC Research)
documents.title: Considerations for Responsible Use and Recommendations for Generative AI in Research and Education
documents.summary: A landing page summarizing the committee's charge, approach and Points to Consider framework, with the full report in a linked PDF that is not in the text. It sets no rules on student AI use.
documents.stance_why: The page describes a committee charge to articulate a "positive but careful approach" and recommends a "living framework", but states no rule on AI use, so it sets no stance and defers.

units.why: The charge asks the committee to "Articulate a 'positive but careful approach' to Generative AI", an institution-level statement of stance and principles, so P56.
units.anchor: positive but careful approach

units.why: The charge includes "Conduct benchmarking with peer institutions regarding policies or guidance on GenAI uses", which is benchmarking against peers, P88.
units.anchor: Conduct benchmarking with peer institutions regarding policies or guidance on GenAI uses

units.why: The charge asks to "Identify key areas in which Pitt can position itself as a leader in the GenAI arena", a commitment to institutional AI leadership; P122 is nearest but this names strategy, not funding or infrastructure.
units.anchor: Identify key areas in which Pitt can position itself as a leader
units.fit_note: States an aim to lead in AI rather than a commitment of research centers, resources or funding.

units.why: The committee records that AI "holds potential to promote equity, improve efficiency, enhance learning, expand knowledge", naming benefits without a rule, so P87.
units.anchor: holds potential to promote equity, improve efficiency, enhance learning, expand knowledge

units.why: The committee notes that "the normative questions—the 'whether' and 'if so, how' questions" attend AI use, framing the decision as one to weigh in context; P118 is nearest.
units.anchor: the importance of considering the normative questions
units.fit_note: Frames whether and how to use AI as normative questions to examine; does not tell users to weigh benefits and risks.

units.why: The committee says it "continue to review the GenAI/AI landscape at least annually", a recurring review commitment, P54.
units.anchor: continue to review the GenAI/AI landscape at least annually

units.why: The range of uses, norms and the technology are "rapidly evolving", given as the reason the framework is a "living framework"; this is a statement that the guidance is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: may serve as a “living framework” for future deliberations
units.fit_note: Also states that the technology and its uses are rapidly evolving as the reason.

units.why: "Points to Consider in addressing concerns or developing policy regarding GenAI" is an institution-level framework for policy-making, P56.
units.anchor: Points to Consider in addressing concerns or developing policy regarding GenAI

units.why: "The Committee urges that these Points to Consider be employed when implementing its Recommendations" asks implementers to apply the framework, P56.
units.anchor: The Committee urges that these Points to Consider be employed

units.why: The committee was "constituted and charged by former Provost Cudd, Interim Provost McCarthy, and SVC Rutenbar", describing who created the body that produced the guidance, P84.
units.anchor: constituted and charged by former Provost Cudd, Interim Provost McCarthy, and SVC Rutenbar
units.frag_start: The Ad Hoc Committee on Generative

units.why: The report is grounded in a "Mapping Project exploring faculty perspectives on GenAI through surveys and focus groups in eight Pitt units"; evidence was gathered, P55, though about perspectives rather than learning outcomes.
units.anchor: Mapping Project exploring faculty perspectives on GenAI through surveys and focus groups
units.fit_note: Evidence on faculty perspectives, not on how AI affects student learning.

units.why: The "Journal and Publisher Policies Project examining policies regarding use of GenAI in academic publishing" is a review of research-publication AI rules; P62 is nearest but the passage only reports the examination, not a rule.
units.anchor: Journal and Publisher Policies Project examining policies regarding use of GenAI in academic publishing
units.fit_note: Describes a review of publisher policies; no AI rule for research is stated.

documents.title: Swanson School of Engineering Academic Integrity Policy: Students and Faculty Obligations and Hearing Procedures
documents.summary: The school integrity policy lists AI inside its definitions of violations: unauthorized AI help in evaluation, AI dependence the instructor prohibits, unacknowledged AI work and passing off AI work as one's own. The remainder is hearing procedure with no AI-specific content.
documents.stance_why: AI help in evaluations is a violation "in a manner not authorized by the instructor" and in other work only where "expressly prohibited by the instructor", so permission rests with instructors and the document sets no single stance.

units.why: Violation 3 lists receiving "assistance during academic evaluation from another person or artificial intelligence in a manner not authorized by the instructor", so unauthorized AI help in evaluation is a violation (default restrictive: banned unless the instructor authorizes). I chose P36 (classified as integrity violation) over P22 because it does not name exams.
units.anchor: Receives assistance during academic evaluation from another person or artificial intelligence in a manner

units.why: Violation 8 covers dependence on "artificial intelligence in a manner expressly prohibited by the instructor" in preparing work for credit; AI is a violation only where the instructor prohibits it, so this ties the rule to instructor decisions. P36 over P04 because it is listed as an integrity violation.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence in a manner expressly prohibited by the instructor

units.why: Violation 10 treats presenting the words of "artificial intelligence without customary and proper acknowledgement of sources" as a violation, so AI must be acknowledged; P24 (disclose/cite AI use) with the violation framing.
units.anchor: persons, or artificial intelligence without customary and proper acknowledgement of sources.

units.why: Violation 11 forbids submitting "the work of another person or artificial intelligence in a manner which represents the work to be one's own", i.e. having AI produce submitted work as your own, P19.
units.anchor: Submits the work of another person or artificial intelligence in a manner which

notes: Thin AI text. The CTL page text is a landing page (tile blurbs only); the committee page excludes the PDF report. In the SSOE PDF, 'AI' in the hearing procedures means 'academic integrity'; generic sanctions and hearing procedures were not coded because they are not AI-specific.
